title: Strength with wisdom
hookLine: Hanuman answers a gift, a test and a danger three different ways, and why Hindus pray to him for wisdom
carry: pray to hanuman for wisdom, not only strength

cards: Simhika's mouth is open wide beneath him, the same trap Surasa set yesterday, only this time there's no blessing waiting at the end. Hanuman has one trick that already worked.
Strong as he is, the question for him isn't how hard to hit. It's what this moment really is, and what it needs. Watch how differently he answers her.

teach.h: INTO THE MOUTH, AND OUT AGAIN.
teach.b: Simhika opens her mouth wide, and at first Hanuman does what worked with Surasa. He makes himself huge, and she opens wider. Then he makes himself small and drops straight into her mouth.
But this time he doesn't dart back out with a bow. Inside her, Valmiki says, he tears at her vital organs, then shoots out again, quick as thought. Simhika falls dead into the sea.
The beings watching from the sky cheer, and they give him a line worth keeping: whoever has, as you do, these four, steadiness, insight, intelligence and skill, does not fail at the work.
Set the three meetings side by side. Mainaka offered rest, and Hanuman answered with courtesy. Surasa set the gods' test, and he answered with wit.
Simhika was simply a danger, and he answered with force. Same Hanuman, three answers, each right because he saw clearly first. That's why Hindus pray to Hanuman for more than muscle.
The Hanuman Chalisa, the hymn so many families know by heart, opens by asking him for strength, wisdom and knowledge: bal, buddhi, vidya.
In this tradition strength alone is never the ideal; the ideal is strength guided by wisdom.
Then Hanuman looks ahead and sees it at last: the far shore, a line of hills, and beyond them a city.
He comes down on a mountain at the water's edge, and Valmiki notes that after a hundred yojanas he isn't even out of breath.

how: Many families recite the Hanuman Chalisa, whose opening asks Hanuman for strength, wisdom and knowledge; readers of the Sundara Kanda point to the verse praising his steadiness, insight, intelligence and skill.

o: the shadow-catcher Hanuman defeats from inside
the serpent mother who blesses Hanuman's crossing
the guardian spirit at the gate of Lanka

p: wisdom, asked of Hanuman in prayer

s: Hanuman defeats Simhika exactly the way he passed Surasa
he enters her mouth again, but this time he tears her from inside.
the watching beings praise steadiness, insight, intelligence and skill
they say whoever has these four does not fail.
the Hanuman Chalisa asks him only for strength
it asks for strength, wisdom and knowledge: bal, buddhi, vidya.

games.q: you're Hanuman. Simhika has opened her mouth wide. you passed Surasa by slipping in and out with a bow. what does this moment need?
o: force: she's a danger, not a test from the gods.
games.why: he reads her for what she is, no test, just a danger, so he goes in small and destroys her from inside. strength guided by insight.

practice: If you know the Hanuman Chalisa, or only its opening, say it slowly now, and when you reach strength, wisdom and knowledge, mean the middle one.

If you don't pray, think of one choice waiting for you this week and ask only: what is this, really, and what does it need? Then let the breath come and go, steady, as Hanuman lands without being out of breath.

wordCard.voice: Simhika. The shadow-catcher whom Hanuman defeats from the inside, the third of three meetings over the sea, each answered in a different way.

orig.note: Sanskrit dhṛti, steadiness: the first of the four qualities praised after Simhika's defeat.

carryVoice: Your line: pray to Hanuman for wisdom, not only strength. Ahead, a city waits for nightfall. Day six hundred eleven, done.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 1 (Simhika's defeat; the four qualities; arrival on the shore)
